## Yesterday in 30 seconds
`touch` creates empty files, `mkdir` creates folders and `mkdir -p` creates a whole path at once.

## Why this matters
Copying and moving files is most of what you do in a terminal: backing up a config before editing it, renaming a script, tidying a downloads folder.

## The concept
**`cp SOURCE DEST`** copies. The original stays where it is. **`mv SOURCE DEST`** moves, and because a rename is just a move inside the same folder, `mv` is also how you rename.

Both overwrite an existing destination without asking. Add `-i` to be asked first.

## Commands

### Copy a file
```bash
cp notes.txt notes.bak
ls
```
```output
notes.bak  notes.txt
```

### Copy a folder with -r
```bash
cp -r project project-backup
```

### Rename with mv
```bash
mv notes.bak old-notes.txt
ls
```
```output
notes.txt  old-notes.txt
```

> ⚠️ `cp` and `mv` replace an existing file with the same name silently. Use `cp -i` and `mv -i` while you're learning.

## Cheat sheet
| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `cp a b` | Copy file a to b |
| `cp -r dir1 dir2` | Copy a folder and everything in it |
| `mv a b` | Move or rename a to b |
| `mv -i a b` | Ask before overwriting |

> 💡 On WSL, keep your work under `~` rather than `/mnt/c`: copies inside the Linux filesystem are much faster.

quiz.q: After `cp a.txt b.txt`, what happens to `a.txt`?
quiz.explain: cp copies; the source is untouched.

quiz.q: How do you rename a file in Linux?
quiz.explain: A rename is a move within the same folder, so mv does it.

quiz.q: Why does `cp project backup` fail when `project` is a folder?
options: cp needs -r to copy a folder

quiz.q: `b.txt` already exists. What does `mv a.txt b.txt` do?
quiz.explain: mv overwrites silently unless you pass -i.

quiz.q: Type the command that copies the folder `site` to `site-backup`, including everything inside it.
Type the command that renames `draft.md` to `final.md` and asks before overwriting.
quiz.explain: -i asks before replacing an existing file.
